searchText: <@508125616940515329> > Are there use cases for different code being deposited to the same account? How would this pattern look like? (within 2 different transactions) Initially, I wanted temporary accounts to be able to handle callbacks. However, this would effectively give temporary accounts the same functionality as persistent accounts, except that they would only exist for the duration of a transaction. This functionality is already possible with CREATEx/SELFDESTRUCT, but the cost is currently too high. I think if the idea of temporary accounts had come up earlier, EIP-1014 might have introduced TCREATE instead of CREATE2. With TCREATE, we can emulate all of the deployment patterns currently available on the network using just the TCREATE/CREATE pair. Therefore, prohibiting CREATE2 would be reasonable if the goal is to simplify deployment semantics. A more radical idea would be to change CREATE2 so that the created account is automatically deleted at the end of the transaction. However, this would break existing CREATE2 factories. In that model: CREATE3: TCREATE → CREATE CREATE2: Similar to CREATE3, but fix the initcode. I want to point out that even without native ephemeral accounts in Glamsterdam, transaction throughput per block is still relatively high. At the 100M gas equilibrium target, we can create around 544 accounts per block, with a maximum of 1,089 accounts. If each account carries code and we assume a cost of 2M gas per account, we could create around 50 accounts at the equilibrium target and up to 100 accounts per block. Overall, this may be sufficient during the period when ephemeral accounts are being researched and deployed, especially given that the post-Glamsterdam base fee is relatively low most of the time. The main issue is during periods of network congestion, or with how wallet interfaces suggest transaction fees. For example, MetaMask always suggests a 1.5 gwei priority fee unless the user adjusts it manually. This can have a noticeable impact on UX. Optimizations in Hegota should significantly reduce this burden in those cases. <@968526635735326741> We should also evaluate ephemeral accounts based on their potential demand, rather than historical usage. Otherwise, we may end up having this use case unnecessarily compete for resources with other use cases that also consume state. Double-clicking is really annoying

excerpts.author: gaxanh
excerpts.content:
I want to point out that even without native ephemeral accounts in Glamsterdam, transaction throughput per block is still relatively high.

At the 100M gas equilibrium target, we can create around 544 accounts per block, with a maximum of 1,089 accounts. If each account carries code and we assume a cost of 2M gas per account, we could create around 50 accounts at the equilibrium target and up to 100 accounts per block. Overall, this may be sufficient during the period when ephemeral accounts are being researched and deployed, especially given that the post-Glamsterdam base fee is relatively low most of the time.

The main issue is during periods of network congestion, or with how wallet interfaces suggest transaction fees. For example, MetaMask always suggests a 1.5 gwei priority fee unless the user adjusts it manually. This can have a noticeable impact on UX. Optimizations in Hegota should significantly reduce this burden in those cases.

<@968526635735326741> We should also evaluate ephemeral accounts based on their potential demand, rather than historical usage. Otherwise, we may end up having this use case unnecessarily compete for resources with other use cases that also consume state.
